segments.text: Elastic 9.4 just dropped, with ESQL support for time series data in GA, a tech preview
of ESQ sub queries, and the disk BBQ vector index now becoming the default.
These changes will improve how you work with logs and metrics, how you perform complex
analyses, and how efficiently your vector databases use resources.
So let's get into it.
Here's the situation a lot of teams end up in.
Your logs are in Elasticsearch, your metrics are in a separate time series system, and
when something goes wrong at 2am, you're jumping between the 2.
tools, to query languages, and to time context, trying to correlate signals that don't naturally
line up.
This is the gap that time series support in ESQL closes, so we're really excited to announce
it's going GA in Elasticsearch 9.4.
This means that you can now analyze filter and aggregate metrics directly with ESQL.
You can perform run rate calculations, rolling window aggregations, and cumulative sums
without any context switching.
The TS command gives you native time series querying, with functions like
rate, cumulative sum, changes and tier range, all available and production supported.
More concretely, it means your logs and metrics can now live together in Elasticsearch, where a single query
can analyze both.
One language, one time context, one place to look when something goes wrong.
The TS command was available as a tech preview in 9.2 and 9.3, so some of you might be familiar
with it already.
It is now generally available as of 9.4, so you can use it for monitoring, alerting and reporting
with the confidence of a fully supported, stable capability.
9.4 also introduces a tech preview of sub queries to ESQL, adding the ability to express multi-stage logic
as one query. Say, if you want to find the set of users who did X, then analyze their behavior across Y.
That used to be two queries with a manual handoff. You run the first, extract the results set,
paste those values as a filter into the second. It's a friction point that slows down every investigation,
and introduces room for error.
Subquiries let you express that entire chain as a single ESQL statement.
The inner query runs first to produce a result set, and the outer query filters against it,
all in a single execution. That moves the manual handoff between steps, and with it the manual
source of errors in this kind of investigation. Subquiries land in 9.4 as a tech preview.
Try them out and give us your feedback. We'd love to know what you think about it.
9.4 also makes a small change with
big impact to Lastic's vector index. This BBQ is now the default vector indexing and
search algorithm. This is a big deal if you're using Lasticsearch's vector capabilities for
semantic search, RAG, or AI-powered applications. This BBQ gives you a highly memory-efficient
vector index that significantly reduces the memory footprint and indexing time compared to HNSW.
Meaning your vector index will cost a lot less and reduce the time between data ingestion and
search availability. All at a very comparative
recorded recall and search latency. We think that this is a sensible default that'll
serve the majority of users really well. HNSW remains a great option if you want that
extra bit of recall and search latency, just remember to specify it in your indexing options.
If working with logs and metrics for monitoring and diagnoses or multi-stage query
logic is important to you, these new features in Elasticsearch 6.4 will change how you work with
your data. The time series capabilities going GA and sub queries will make your analyses faster,
more reliable and easier than ever. And for everybody building semantic search,
rag or AI powered applications, the small nudge towards the disk bbq index will have huge cost
and indexing speed implications. If you've yet to try out disk bbq, you might be missing out
on a potential order of magnitude reduction in memory use and indexing time. This is a great time
to try out these features with 9.4.
ESQL documentation and the 9.4 release notes are in the description. We'll leave links to the
S command and sub queries in ESQ as well as links to disk bbq references. I'd love to
hear about your experiences with these features or 9.4 in general. So drop your experience in the
comments and we'd love to know what questions you run into. Thanks for watching. See you next time.
